title: Definitive guidelines for registering community/open models in the catalog
creator: Diego Ramirez
description: Clarify and lock down the acceptance criteria, required metadata, and compatibility notes for adding community / open-source models to the Redwood Model Catalog. This ticket captures the product-side rules that engineering and model operations will implement, plus the UI/API surface changes required to expose pinning and compatibility metadata to customers.
background: We have onboarding guidance scattered across PRDs and internal notes. Recent incidents (ENG-4457) showed unclear compatibility metadata caused a failed private deployment when a community model relied on custom fused kernels. PM needs a single source of truth for: required metadata, pinning semantics, supported variants, and documented compatibility constraints so that on-call and customers avoid surprises.
scope: Define required model registration fields shown in Console and returned by Catalog API
Specify default and optional version pinning policies and human-readable labels
Enumerate compatibility checks (runtime ops, tokenizer, kv-cache format, sequence length, quantization support)
Define UX copy for Console onboarding flow and API examples
Acceptance criteria and test definitions for catalog onboarding automation
out_of_scope: Automated kernel fusion or build-time patching of community models (ENG to decide separately)
Changes to offline model training pipelines
Pricing or billing model changes for hosted/dedicated tiers
requirements: Every community model entry must include: canonical name, semantic version tag, license (SPDX), primary framework (PyTorch/TF/JAX), tokenizer type and vocabulary hash, max_sequence_length, kv_cache_format (simple/packed), quantization_variants (if provided), and suggested default variant
Registration UI and Catalog API must expose a 'compatibility_score' (0-100) and a short 'compatibility_notes' string summarizing known runtime caveats

Pinning options: 'floating' (always use latest compatible minor), 'major-locked' (lock major semver), 'exact' (exact version only). Default for community models should be 'major-locked' with opt-in to 'floating'
Compatibility checks run at registration: tokenizer mismatch detection, unsupported ops list against runtime kernel catalog, max_seq > runtime max -> flag, quantization metadata validation
A standardized testing checklist (unit prompts + smoke generation) must run before model status moves to 'verified' in the catalog
Console must show a prominent warning for models that require custom ops or nonstandard kernels and disable one-click private deployment unless 'trusted by Redwood' flag is set
APIs that accept model identifiers should allow optional pin query param (e.g., ?pin=exact:1.2.3) and fallback behavior must be documented
acceptance_criteria: PRD is reviewed and approved by Eng leads (runtime + ops), Security, and DX
Catalog API schema updated and backward-compatible; API contract doc published in the API spec repository
Console UI mockups implemented in a design PR and validated with 2 PM customer interviews
Automated registration pipeline runs the compatibility checks and blocks publishing when critical incompatibilities are present

End-to-end test: register a community model with tokenizer mismatch -> registration fails with clear error; register a compatible quantized variant -> passes and appears in catalog with correct metadata
Documentation pages (Public docs + internal runbook) exist and link to sample GitHub onboarding template and checklist
decisions_and_tradeoffs: Default pin policy chosen as 'major-locked' to balance stability with bugfix accessibility; tradeoff: customers who want bleeding-edge must opt-in

Expose a compatibility_score (heuristic) instead of a binary 'supported' flag to reflect probabilistic runtime behavior — risk: customers may misinterpret scores; mitigated via explanatory tooltip and playbook
Require SPDX license metadata to reduce legal risk; tradeoff: increases friction for community contributors who omit license info

Block on critical unsupported ops at registration rather than attempting runtime fallback to minimize production incidents; tradeoff: may prevent some models that would work with future runtime changes
